content: 1. Nutritional Outcomes and Legume Consumption: The frequency of legume consumption was not associated with wasting, underweight, or stunting in children. These findings were derived from observational studies, with varying levels of evidence certainty. 2. Age Determination: The age of infants was determined through interviews with their mothers. 3. Anemia and Bean Consumption: The consumption of beans was not significantly associated with the prevalence of anemia. Anemia was assessed using capillary blood samples obtained via heel or finger puncture, with hemoglobin levels below 11 g/dL used as the diagnostic threshold. Among those consuming beans daily or less frequently, 9% were anemic. 4. Study on Complementary Feeding in Indonesia (Ahmad et al., 2018): This cross-sectional study conducted in Aceh, Indonesia, included 392 healthy children aged 6–23 months. Mothers provided dietary information through repeated 24-hour recalls. The study assessed wasting, underweight, and stunting as outcomes. The study was rated as having good internal validity but noted limitations in sample size and lack of confidence intervals. 5. Study on Anemia Risk Factors in Brazil (Silva et al., 2007): This cross-sectional study included 205 children aged 6–12 months in Viçosa, Brazil. Anemia was defined as hemoglobin levels below 11 g/dL. The study had methodological limitations, including a small sample size, lack of detailed methodology, and no adjustment for confounding variables. It was rated as having poor to fair quality. 6. Study on Nutritional Status in China (Chang et al., 2007): This cross-sectional study analyzed data from the China Food and Nutrition Surveillance System, including 13,107 infants aged 6–24 months. The frequency of fruit and vegetable consumption was associated with stunting and underweight prevalence. However, the study lacked a detailed methods section, and results should be interpreted cautiously. 7. Study on Food Consumption and Growth in Senegal (Ntab et al., 2005): This cross-sectional study included 543 children aged 6–42 months in rural Senegal. Food consumption was assessed through 24-hour recalls and weekly frequency reports. It was rated as fair quality. 8. Study on Iron Status in Norway (Wandel et al., 1996): This cross-sectional study included 74 healthy infants in Norway. Dietary data were collected using a food frequency questionnaire. Iron status was assessed based on serum ferritin levels. The study had a small sample size and limited methodological details, leading to a poor quality rating. 9. Longitudinal Study on Fruit and Vegetable Intake in Norway (Bjelland et al., 2013): This study used data from the Norwegian Mother and Child Cohort Study, including 9,025 mother-infant pairs. The study tracked changes in fruit and vegetable intake over time. Despite its large sample size, the study had methodological limitations and was rated as poor quality. 10. Overall Observations: Many of the studies reviewed had significant methodological limitations, including small sample sizes, lack of detailed methods, and failure to adjust for confounding variables. These issues reduce the certainty of the evidence and necessitate cautious interpretation of the results.
